slides.title: Atomic Structure & Radioactive Isotopes (Carbon-14)
slides.purpose: Construct a neutral Carbon-14 atom using protons, neutrons, and simplified first-20 energy-level filling.
onScreenText: Carbon-14: Z = 6 protons, A = 14
Isotopes differ only in neutron count
Carbon-14 is radioactive (beta emitter)

visual.altText: Carbon-14 nuclide notation showing mass number 14 and atomic number 6
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="44" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">¹⁴₆C — Carbon-14 Isotope</text><text x="400" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#4338ca">6 protons · 8 neutrons · 6 electrons (2, 4)</text></svg>

narration.script: Build a neutral Carbon-14 atom by setting its protons, neutrons, and electron energy levels.

keyIdeas: Proton count defines the element; neutron count defines the isotope.

interactive.title: Build a Neutral Carbon-14 Atom
interactive.instructions: Set protons, neutrons, and energy-level electrons to build neutral Carbon-14 (A = 14, Z = 6).
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Atomic structure builder for Carbon-14 isotope
interactive.fallbackText: Neutral Carbon-14 has 6 protons, 8 neutrons (mass number 14), and 6 electrons arranged 2, 4 across energy levels 1 and 2. Carbon-14 is a radioactive isotope used in radiocarbon dating.
interactive.modelNote: Simplified first-20-element ground-state filling model (up to 2, 8, 8, 2). Energy-level rings represent quantised energies, not circular tracks.

prediction.prompt: Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons. What changes to make Carbon-14?
prediction.explanation: Isotopes of the same element always have the same number of protons (6 for carbon) and differ only in neutrons (8 for Carbon-14).

hints: Keep protons at 6 so it remains carbon.
Set neutrons to 14 - 6 = 8 and place 6 electrons as 2, 4.

slides.title: AS/A-Level Subshells — Iron(II) Ion (Fe²⁺)
slides.purpose: Apply 4s-before-3d cation ionisation to construct the ground-state subshell configuration of Fe²⁺.
onScreenText: Fe (Z = 26): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s²
Transition-metal cations lose 4s electrons before 3d
Fe²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁶

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="44" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Fe²⁺ Subshell Configuration</text><text x="400" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#4338ca">26 protons · 24 electrons · Remove 4s before 3d</text></svg>

narration.script: Construct the ground-state subshell occupancy of the iron(II) ion, remembering which subshell loses electrons first.

keyIdeas: When transition metals ionise, 4s electrons are removed before 3d electrons.

interactive.title: Build the Fe²⁺ Ion Subshell Configuration
interactive.instructions: Adjust the subshell occupancies (1s through 3d) for Fe²⁺ (Z = 26, 24 electrons).
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Subshell occupancy builder for Iron(II) ion
interactive.fallbackText: Neutral Fe (Z = 26) is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s². Removing two electrons to form Fe²⁺ removes both 4s electrons first, yielding 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ ([Ar] 3d⁶).
interactive.modelNote: AS/A-Level subshell occupancy model (Z = 1..30). Tracks subshell totals rather than individual degenerate orbital spin boxes.
hints: Start from neutral Fe (26 e⁻) and remove 2 electrons from 4s, not 3d.

slides.title: Ionic Bonding — Sodium Chloride (NaCl)
slides.purpose: Transfer 1 outer electron from Na to Cl to form Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in a 1:1 lattice ratio.
onScreenText: Empirical ratio 1:1 in a giant ionic lattice

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="44" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Sodium Chloride (NaCl)</text><text x="400" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#0f766e">Electron transfer → [Na]⁺ and [Cl]⁻ in a giant ionic lattice</text></svg>

narration.script: Transfer sodium's outer electron to chlorine and observe how both ions achieve full outer shells.

keyIdeas: Ionic bonding involves electron transfer and electrostatic attraction across a giant lattice.

interactive.title: Form Sodium Chloride (NaCl)
interactive.instructions: Select the simplest whole-number ratio of Na and Cl atoms and transfer the outer electron.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Ionic bonding electron transfer builder for sodium chloride
interactive.fallbackText: One Na atom transfers 1 outer electron to one Cl atom, forming [Na]⁺ and [Cl]⁻ in a 1:1 empirical ratio (NaCl) within a giant ionic lattice.
interactive.modelNote: Empirical formula unit only — solid NaCl is an extended three-dimensional ionic lattice, not an isolated diatomic molecule.

slides.title: Ionic Formula Ratios — Aluminium Oxide (Al₂O₃)
slides.purpose: Balance a 5-ion empirical formula ratio (2 Al³⁺ : 3 O²⁻) with 6 transferred electrons.
onScreenText: Each Al loses 3 e⁻ → Al³⁺
Each O gains 2 e⁻ → O²⁻
Simplest neutral ratio: Al₂O₃ (6 electrons transferred)

visual.altText: Aluminium oxide 2 to 3 ionic ratio overview
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="44" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Aluminium Oxide (Al₂O₃)</text><text x="400" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#0f766e">2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0 · 6 electrons transferred</text></svg>

narration.script: Find the simplest neutral ratio of aluminium and oxygen ions and transfer all six outer electrons.

keyIdeas: Total positive charge must equal total negative charge in the simplest whole-number ratio.

interactive.title: Construct Aluminium Oxide (Al₂O₃)
interactive.instructions: Set the simplest whole-number ratio of Al and O atoms (up to 6 ions total) and transfer the required electrons.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Ionic bonding builder for aluminium oxide
interactive.fallbackText: Two Al atoms lose 3 electrons each (6 e⁻ total) to three O atoms (2 e⁻ each), producing 2 Al³⁺ and 3 O²⁻ in the empirical formula Al₂O₃.
interactive.modelNote: Represents the 2:3 empirical composition of solid Al₂O₃ giant ionic lattice.

slides.title: Single Covalent Bonding — Chlorine (Cl₂)
slides.purpose: Share one electron pair between two chlorine atoms and assign 3 lone pairs to each.
onScreenText: Each Cl has 7 valence electrons (14 total)
1 shared pair (single bond) + 3 lone pairs per Cl

visual.altText: Chlorine molecule single covalent bond overview
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="44" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Chlorine (Cl₂)</text><text x="400" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#0284c7">14 valence electrons · 1 single bond · 3 lone pairs each</text></svg>

narration.script: Connect the two chlorine atoms with a single covalent bond and add their non-bonding lone pairs.

keyIdeas: Non-metals share electron pairs to complete octets.

interactive.title: Build Chlorine (Cl₂)
interactive.instructions: Form a single Cl–Cl bond and place the non-bonding lone pairs so all 14 valence electrons are conserved.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Covalent bonding builder for chlorine molecule
interactive.fallbackText: In Cl₂, two Cl atoms share 1 bonding pair (2 e⁻) and each keeps 3 lone pairs (6 e⁻), giving each Cl an octet of 8 electrons.

slides.title: Multiple Covalent Bonds — Oxygen (O₂) & Nitrogen (N₂)
slides.purpose: Compare double (O=O) and triple (N≡N) covalent bonding in two independent activities on one slide.
onScreenText: O₂: double bond + 2 lone pairs per O
N₂: triple bond + 1 lone pair per N
Note: Lewis model does not explain O₂ paramagnetism

visual.altText: Oxygen double bond and nitrogen triple bond comparison
visual.description: O2 and N2 multiple bond header.
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="44" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Multiple Bonds: O₂ & N₂</text><text x="400" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#0284c7">Double bond (4 shared e⁻) vs Triple bond (6 shared e⁻)</text></svg>

narration.script: Construct both the double-bonded oxygen molecule and the triple-bonded nitrogen molecule below.

keyIdeas: Atoms can share two or three pairs of electrons to satisfy the octet model.

interactive.title: Build Oxygen (O₂) — Double Bond
interactive.instructions: Form a double bond between the two oxygen atoms and place 2 lone pairs on each oxygen.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Covalent bonding builder for oxygen double bond
interactive.fallbackText: In the Lewis model of O₂ (12 valence electrons), the two O atoms share 2 pairs (O=O) and each holds 2 lone pairs. Note: introductory Lewis structures cannot explain O₂'s experimental paramagnetism (which requires molecular orbital theory).
interactive.modelNote: Introductory Lewis model — does not account for the paramagnetism of O₂ observed experimentally.

interactive.title: Build Nitrogen (N₂) — Triple Bond
interactive.instructions: Form a triple bond between the two nitrogen atoms and place 1 lone pair on each nitrogen.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Covalent bonding builder for nitrogen triple bond
interactive.fallbackText: In N₂ (10 valence electrons), the two N atoms share 3 pairs (N≡N) and each holds 1 lone pair.

slides.title: Lewis Structures — Ammonia (NH₃)
slides.purpose: Construct NH₃ with 3 N–H single bonds and 1 central lone pair on nitrogen.
onScreenText: NH₃: 8 valence electrons
3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair on N

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="44" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Ammonia (NH₃)</text><text x="400" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#0284c7">8 valence electrons · 3 N–H bonds + 1 lone pair on N</text></svg>

narration.script: Build the Lewis structure of ammonia, making sure nitrogen keeps its lone pair.

keyIdeas: Nitrogen's lone pair in NH₃ is available for coordinate bonding.

interactive.title: Build Ammonia (NH₃)
interactive.instructions: Connect nitrogen to all three hydrogen atoms and assign nitrogen's non-bonding lone pair.
interactive.fallbackText: Ammonia (NH₃) has 8 valence electrons: 3 single N–H bonds (6 e⁻) and 1 lone pair (2 e⁻) on nitrogen.

slides.title: Coordinate (Dative) Bonding — NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺
slides.purpose: Donate nitrogen's lone pair in NH₃ to an incoming H⁺ ion to form the ammonium ion NH₄⁺.
onScreenText: Start with NH₃ (1 lone pair on N) + H⁺ (0 electrons)
N donates its lone pair in a dative bond (N→H)
All four N–H bonds in NH₄⁺ are equivalent once formed

visual.altText: Ammonium ion formation by coordinate bonding
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="44" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺</text><text x="400" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#b45309">Coordinate (dative) bond donated by nitrogen's lone pair</text></svg>

narration.script: Start from ammonia and an incoming hydrogen ion. Donate nitrogen's lone pair to form the coordinate bond in ammonium.

keyIdeas: A coordinate bond forms when one atom donates both shared electrons to an electron-deficient acceptor.

interactive.title: Form the Ammonium Ion (NH₄⁺) from NH₃ + H⁺
interactive.instructions: Donate nitrogen's lone pair (reduce N lone pairs from 1 to 0) and form a dative bond (n1 → h4) to the incoming H⁺ ion.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Coordinate covalent bonding builder for ammonium ion
interactive.fallbackText: Nitrogen in NH₃ donates its lone pair to H⁺ via a coordinate (dative) bond, forming NH₄⁺ (8 valence electrons, 4 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs, formal charge +1 on N). Once formed, all four N–H bonds are identical.
interactive.modelNote: Starts from NH₃ (3 bonds + 1 lone pair) and unbonded H⁺ (h4). Once formed, all four N–H bonds in NH₄⁺ are equivalent in length and strength.

slides.title: Octet Exception — Boron Trifluoride (BF₃)
slides.purpose: Demonstrate an electron-deficient covalent molecule where boron has 6 valence electrons.
onScreenText: The octet rule is NOT universal
BF₃: boron has only 6 electrons around it (3 single bonds)
Each fluorine has 1 bond + 3 lone pairs (octet)

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="44" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Boron Trifluoride (BF₃)</text><text x="400" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#0284c7">Electron-deficient central boron (6 valence electrons)</text></svg>

narration.script: Not every molecule obeys the octet rule. Build boron trifluoride, where central boron has only six shared electrons.

keyIdeas: Boron in BF₃ is electron-deficient (6 electrons) and acts as an electron-pair acceptor.

interactive.title: Build Boron Trifluoride (BF₃) — Electron-Deficient Exception
interactive.instructions: Form three single B–F bonds and place 3 lone pairs on each fluorine atom (24 valence electrons total).
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Covalent bonding builder for electron-deficient boron trifluoride
interactive.fallbackText: BF₃ has 24 valence electrons: three B–F single bonds (6 e⁻ around B) and 3 lone pairs on each F atom. Central boron is electron-deficient with 6 electrons.
interactive.modelNote: Atom-specific electron-deficient octet exception (boron: 6 electrons). Fluorine atoms still obey the octet rule.

slides.title: VSEPR Molecular Geometry — Water (H₂O)
slides.purpose: Distinguish tetrahedral electron-domain geometry from bent molecular shape (104.5°).
onScreenText: H₂O: 2 bonding domains + 2 lone pairs = 4 domains
Electron geometry: tetrahedral
Molecular shape: bent (104.5°) · Polar

visual.altText: Water bent molecular geometry with 104.5 degree bond angle
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="44" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Water (H₂O) — VSEPR Shape</text><text x="400" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#0284c7">Tetrahedral electron geometry → Bent molecular shape (104.5°)</text></svg>

narration.script: Use VSEPR theory to distinguish water's electron-domain geometry from its bent molecular shape and polarity.

keyIdeas: Lone-pair repulsion compresses the H–O–H angle from 109.5° to 104.5°.

interactive.title: Water (H₂O): Lone Pairs, Shape & Polarity
interactive.instructions: Set oxygen's bonding domains and lone pairs, choose electron geometry and molecular shape, and classify polarity.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: VSEPR molecular geometry and polarity builder for water
interactive.fallbackText: H₂O has 2 bonding domains and 2 lone pairs (tetrahedral electron geometry, bent molecular shape, reference angle 104.5°). Its two O–H dipoles do not cancel, so water is polar.
interactive.modelNote: Curated VSEPR reference model; bond angle 104.5° is an experimental reference value, not calculated from first-principles quantum mechanics.

slides.title: Mixed-Ligand Molecular Polarity — Chloromethane (CH₃Cl)
slides.purpose: Demonstrate that symmetrical tetrahedral geometry can still be polar when surrounding ligands differ.
onScreenText: CH₄: tetrahedral, identical H ligands → non-polar
CH₃Cl: tetrahedral, one Cl ligand → net dipole → polar

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="44" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Chloromethane (CH₃Cl)</text><text x="400" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#0284c7">Tetrahedral shape with mixed ligands → Overall Polar</text></svg>

narration.script: Compare methane and chloromethane: both are tetrahedral, yet chloromethane is polar because the C–Cl dipole is not cancelled.

keyIdeas: Overall polarity depends on both 3D geometry and ligand electronegativity.

interactive.title: Chloromethane (CH₃Cl): Mixed-Ligand Polarity
interactive.instructions: Set carbon's bonding domains and lone pairs, choose the geometry, and determine whether CH₃Cl is polar.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: VSEPR molecular geometry and polarity builder for chloromethane
interactive.fallbackText: CH₃Cl has 4 bonding domains and 0 lone pairs (tetrahedral). Unlike symmetrical CH₄, the strongly polar C–Cl bond is not cancelled by the three C–H bonds, making CH₃Cl a polar molecule.
interactive.modelNote: Polarity is evaluated via 3D VSEPR unit-vector dipole summation using Pauling electronegativities, not 2D screen coordinates.

slides.title: Intermolecular Forces — Hydrogen Bonding Condition (Reusing Rule Explorer)
slides.purpose: Reuse existing LIVE rule-explorer for IMF classification while emphasising that London dispersion forces act between ALL molecules.
onScreenText: London dispersion forces exist between ALL atoms and molecules
Hydrogen bonding requires H covalently bonded to N, O, or F + a lone pair on N, O, or F
IMFs are additive, not mutually exclusive

visual.altText: Intermolecular forces hierarchy showing London dispersion present in all molecules
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="42" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Intermolecular Forces (IMFs)</text><text x="400" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#0f766e">London dispersion acts in ALL molecules · H-bonding is additional</text></svg>

narration.script: Explore the conditions for hydrogen bonding using the existing Rule Explorer, remembering that London dispersion forces are always present too.

keyIdeas: London dispersion forces occur between all atoms and molecules, including polar molecules.

interactive.title: When Does Hydrogen Bonding Occur (In Addition to London Dispersion Forces)?
interactive.instructions: Toggle both structural conditions to test whether hydrogen bonding occurs between molecules.
interactive.fallbackText: London dispersion forces occur between ALL atoms and molecules (including polar ones). Hydrogen bonding occurs additionally only when a molecule has H covalently bonded to N, O, or F AND a neighbouring N, O, or F atom with a lone pair.

inputs.label: H covalently bonded to N, O, or F
Lone pair on N, O, or F

output.trueLabel: Hydrogen Bonding Present (+ London Dispersion & Permanent Dipole)
output.falseLabel: No Hydrogen Bonding (London Dispersion Still Present)
output.explanationTrue: Both conditions are met: hydrogen bonds form in addition to London dispersion forces and permanent dipole-dipole interactions.
output.explanationFalse: Without both conditions, hydrogen bonding cannot form — though London dispersion forces still act between all molecules (and permanent dipole-dipole interactions if polar).

summary.recapScript: You explored atomic structure, subshells, ionic ratios, covalent and coordinate bonding, VSEPR polarity, and intermolecular forces.
keyTakeaways: Use the right model for each level: introductory shells vs A-Level subshells, empirical ionic lattices, Lewis/octet exceptions, and 3D VSEPR dipole symmetry.
